analysis.one_liner: Halves the tax rate on capital gains and expands small business stock tax breaks.
analysis.headline: Introduced by 5 Republican senators on March 20, 1997, the bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 105th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have let every taxpayer deduct half of their capital gains from income, cutting the tax on profits from selling stocks, businesses, and property roughly in half (the bill's own text drops example rates from 28% to 17.5%). It would also have raised the tax-free share of gains on "qualified small business stock" from 50% to 75%, cut the required holding period from five years to three, let corporations claim the exclusion, doubled the asset limit for qualifying businesses to $100 million, and adjusted the value of long-held assets for inflation so less of the sale counts as taxable gain. One narrower provision would have let homeowners deduct a loss on selling their principal residence.
analysis.who_benefits: Households and corporations with taxable capital gains — a benefit concentrated heavily among the wealthiest Americans, since most capital gains income goes to top earners. Investors in qualified small business stock would gain the most: a 75% tax-free share of gains after just three years, the ability to roll gains tax-free into new small business stock, and looser eligibility rules. Mutual funds, REITs, partnerships, and S corporations would pass all of these new breaks through to their investors under the bill's pass-through rules. Homeowners who sell their house for less than they paid would gain a new loss deduction.

how_it_helps.text: Gives all taxpayers a 50% deduction for net capital gains, roughly halving the tax on profits from selling stocks, businesses, and other assets; the bill's own conforming amendments show the relevant tax rates falling from 28% to 17.5%.

Raises the tax-free exclusion for gains on qualified small business stock from 50% to 75%, cuts the required holding period from five years to three, extends the exclusion to corporations, doubles the qualifying asset ceiling to $100 million with inflation adjustments, repeals the per-issuer cap, and lets investors roll gains tax-free into new small business stock.
Adjusts the tax basis of stock and tangible property held more than three years for inflation, so gains that merely track rising prices would no longer be taxed.
Allows a capital loss deduction when a homeowner sells a principal residence for less than its purchase price — the bill's only provision aimed at ordinary households rather than investors.

analysis.who_pays: The U.S. Treasury and, ultimately, all federal taxpayers. Halving capital gains taxation, expanding small business stock exclusions, and indexing asset values to inflation would each drain federal revenue; the benefits would flow to capital-gains earners while the cost — in higher future taxes, more borrowing, or lower spending — falls on the general public.
analysis.who_pays_short: All federal taxpayers through lost revenue

drawbacks.text: The core benefit — a 50% deduction on capital gains, made available to corporations as well as individuals — flows overwhelmingly to the highest-income households, since capital gains income is concentrated at the top, while the revenue cost is shared by everyone.

The small business stock provisions would be costly and loosely targeted: the exclusion rises to 75% after only three years, the qualifying asset limit doubles to $100 million, the per-issuer cap is repealed, and corporations become eligible, favoring holders of existing stakes over new investment.

Indexing asset values to inflation for all stock and tangible property held over three years would permanently shrink the tax base on investment gains and add substantial complexity, with special rules for short sales, related-party deals, funds, and trusts throughout the bill text.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill contains one genuinely defensible idea — letting homeowners who sell at a loss deduct that loss, a break available today for almost every other kind of investment loss. But its core is a very large tax cut for gains that already flow disproportionately to the wealthiest households, deepened by expanded small business stock exclusions and inflation indexing that would permanently shrink the tax base. Whatever investment stimulus it might produce would come at a revenue cost borne by everyone, with the proceeds concentrated among a few.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate sent it to the Finance Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and it died quietly when the Congress ended in January 1999.

narrative.text: Sen. Connie Mack introduced the bill on March 20, 1997, joined by four Republican cosponsors: Shelby, Cochran, D'Amato, and Hagel.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance on the day of introduction; that referral was the last action ever taken.
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote followed, and the bill expired when the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: General taxpayers were spared a large tax cut aimed at the wealthiest households. Wealthy investors and small business stockholders lost their best chance at the tax breaks, though Congress pursued similar capital gains cuts through other vehicles later in 1997.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: General taxpayers; wealthy investors missed their cut

for.name: Sen. Connie Mack, III
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on March 20, 1997.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee (Chair William Roth)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on March 20, 1997 and took no further action — no hearing, markup, or vote — for the remainder of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever recorded; all five sponsors were Republicans and no Democrat is on record supporting or opposing the bill.

industries.industry: Investors in stock and mutual funds
industries.note: The 50% capital gains deduction and inflation indexing would sharply cut taxes on investment gains, with pass-through rules routing the breaks through regulated investment companies to fund shareholders. The beneficiaries are concentrated at the top; the revenue cost is public.

industries.industry: Venture capital and small business stockholders
industries.note: A 75% tax-free share of gains after just three years, tax-free rollovers into new small business stock, a doubled $100 million asset ceiling, corporate eligibility, and repeal of the per-issuer cap would substantially enrich holders of small business stock. The bill favors existing stakes more than new investment.

REIT investors and owners of tangible business property would gain inflation indexing, while homeowners selling at a loss would gain a new deduction — the bill's one provision aimed at ordinary households rather than asset holders.
